newsitem.title: USA: FTC got 300 e-mails a day on Staples merger.
newsitem.headline: FTC got 300 e-mails a day on Staples merger.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission received 1,662 pieces of electronic mail regarding the proposed merger of Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. in the initial five days of its first invitation for public comment via the Internet, an official said Tuesday.
The amount of e-mail was provided in response to a Freedom of Information Act request from Reuters, but the content was withheld as confidential.
An FTC official said the staff had not finished reading the e-mail, which was being considered as the commission decided what to do next about the proposed $4 billion office superstore merger.
The commission voted 4-1 on March 10 to go to court and try to block the merger.

Two days later, Delray Beach, Fla.-based Office Depot and Westborough, Mass.-based Staples reached an agreement in principle to divest 63 stores to the third player in the field, OfficeMax Inc. of Shaker Heights, Ohio, in an attempt to make the merger acceptable to the FTC.
On March 14, the FTC put a note on its World Wide Web home page at http://www.ftc.gov, inviting e-mail from the public. The note was still there Tuesday.
When the note was first placed on the Web page, an FTC spokeswoman said the e-mails were confidential and sought to play down the invitation, noting that no press release had been issued.
Although the FTC Web page had long invited comments on consumer protection -- its other area of responsibility -- this marked the first time it had invited e-mail on a merger.
The public responded enthusiastically, submitting more than 300 e-mails a day on average during the first five days.

The FTC provided no information on the number of e-mails received since the first five days. An FTC official said commission policy was to provide information only as of the date of the Freedom of Information Act Request, which was March 18, and not during the week it took to respond.
